blocks.prompt: Twenty One Days Inside an Egg
blocks.text: A hen lays an egg and then sits on it. Her warm feathers keep the egg as warm as a bath. Every day she stands up, turns the eggs with her beak, and sits back down. Inside the shell, a chick is slowly growing. It has a yolk for food and a shell for a house. After twenty one days the chick is ready. It has a hard little bump on its beak called an egg tooth. It uses that bump to chip a hole in the shell. Chipping the shell is slow work. The chick rests, then chips again. At last the shell breaks open and the wet chick tumbles out. In a few hours it is dry, fluffy, and running after its mother.

blocks.prompt: The Egg That Breathes
blocks.text: An eggshell looks solid, but it is not. Thousands of tiny holes run through it, far too small for your eye to see. Air moves in through those holes and waste gas moves out. The shell is a house with windows you cannot spot. Inside, a chick is being built out of the yellow yolk and the clear white around it. On the second day of warmth, a heart the size of a pinhead begins to beat. By the end of the first week there are eyes, a beak, and the buds of wings. The hen keeps the egg warm and turns it several times a day so the chick does not stick to one side of the shell. Near day twenty, the chick pokes its beak into a pocket of air at the wide end of the egg and takes its first real breath. Then it starts to peep. A hen will often cluck back to an egg that peeps. On day twenty one the chick chips a ring of holes around the shell and pushes it apart.

blocks.prompt: The Twenty One Day Build
blocks.text: The life cycle of a chicken is a loop with four stages: egg, chick, pullet, hen. The loop begins inside the hen, where a single yolk cell travels down a long tube. Along the way the clear white is layered around it, then two thin skins, then the shell itself, built from calcium and hardened in the last few hours. Start to finish, a hen assembles an egg in roughly twenty five hours. Only an egg fertilized by a rooster can grow a chick. The rest are simply breakfast. If the egg is fertile and stays warm at about one hundred degrees, development begins. The heart beats on day two. Eyes darken by day four. Toes and a beak appear in the second week. Around day nine, a farmer can hold the egg up to a bright light, a trick called candling, and see a dark shape with a web of blood vessels spreading around it. Meanwhile the chick lives entirely off the yolk, and its waste is stored in a sac it will leave behind in the shell. In the last two days the chick swallows what remains of the yolk into its own belly. That stored meal is why a newly hatched chick can go two or three days without eating, and it is the reason day old chicks can travel through the mail. Then comes the hard part. The chick pips a hole with the egg tooth on its beak, rests, and slowly saws a ring around the shell until the top lifts off. Free, wet, and exhausted, it dries into a ball of down. In about five months, if that chick is a hen, she will lay an egg of her own and the loop closes.

blocks.prompt: The Chicken Is a Machine for Making More Chickens
blocks.text: Every chicken alive descends from the red junglefowl, a shy forest bird of Southeast Asia that people began keeping thousands of years ago. The wild bird laid a small clutch once or twice a year. Its descendants now lay almost daily, and there are more chickens on Earth than any other bird. What did not change is the twenty one day process locked inside the shell. An egg is a complete life support system with no way to take on supplies. Everything the chick will need is packed in on the day it is laid: yolk for fuel, albumen for water and protein, a shell of calcium carbonate for armor, and two membranes in between. The shell is drilled with thousands of pores. Oxygen seeps in, carbon dioxide and water vapor seep out, and as water is lost an air cell swells at the blunt end. That air cell is not a flaw. It is the chick's first lungful, waiting for it. Development is fast and strictly ordered. A beating heart appears on day two, before there is a body worth pumping for. Eyes, limb buds, and a beak follow. The hen turns the eggs many times a day, and hatcheries copy her by rocking the trays, because an unturned embryo can fuse to the shell membrane and die. By day nineteen the chick fills nearly the whole shell, curled with its beak tucked under one wing. It pushes through into the air cell, breathes air for the first time, and begins to peep. Hens cluck in reply, and chicks in neighboring eggs adjust their timing so the clutch hatches close together. Hatching is not a crack but a long demolition. The chick pips a single hole, then rotates slowly, chipping as it goes, cutting a ring around the shell over several hours. Finally it kicks the cap off and shoves itself into the world. A chick is precocial, meaning it arrives finished: eyes open, down drying within hours, feet already working. It follows the hen, copies her pecking, and needs no feeding beak to beak. Five or six months later it begins the cycle again, and the shy junglefowl in its ancestry is barely visible at all.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Gallus gallus domesticus, from the red junglefowl
A hen assembles a complete egg in about 25 hours
Shell: roughly 95 percent calcium carbonate
Optimal incubation near 99.5 degrees Fahrenheit
Internal pip on day 19, external pip on day 20
Sex determined by the hen's chromosomes, not the rooster's

blocks.prompt: A Sealed Room With a Deadline
blocks.text: Consider the problem an egg has to solve. A bird cannot carry a growing embryo the way a mammal does, so it must package an entire developmental program into a rigid container, seal it, and walk away for hours at a time. Everything required has to be loaded at the start. Nothing can be added later. The chicken solves this problem twenty one days at a time, and it solves it so reliably that we have stopped noticing. The packaging begins inside the hen. A yolk, which is one enormous cell, is released and travels down a tube called the oviduct. Layers of albumen wrap around it, twisted at each end into cords that suspend the yolk in the middle so it can rotate but not slam against the shell. Two membranes follow. Then the egg spends most of a day in the shell gland, where calcium carbonate is laid down over it in a crystalline sheet. The whole build takes around twenty five hours, and a laying hen begins the next one almost immediately. If a rooster has fertilized the yolk, the embryo is already dividing before the shell is finished, then pauses, waiting for warmth. The finished shell is a compromise. It must be strong enough to bear a sitting hen and weak enough for a chick to break from the inside using nothing but a beak. It must be sealed against bacteria and open to the air, a contradiction it resolves with thousands of microscopic pores. Through those pores oxygen enters and carbon dioxide leaves, and water vapor leaves too, which is the point: as the contents shrink, an air cell inflates at the blunt end. That slowly growing bubble is the chick's first breath, prepared weeks in advance. Development follows a strict timetable. A heart beats on day two, before there is a circulatory system worth the name. Eyes pigment, limb buds sprout, a beak forms. The hen turns the clutch as often as thirty times a day, and this is not fussing. An embryo left unturned can adhere to the shell membrane and die. By day nineteen the chick has run out of room. It draws the last of the yolk sac into its abdomen, a packed lunch that will carry it for two or three days after hatching, then breaks into the air cell and takes a true breath. From inside the shell it begins to peep, and the hen answers. Chicks in adjacent eggs hear each other and shift their pace so the clutch emerges within a few hours of one another, which matters because a hen leads her brood away from the nest once and does not return for stragglers. Hatching itself is deliberate and slow. The chick uses a temporary egg tooth to pip a single hole, rests, then rotates within the shell, chipping a ring until the cap gives way. It emerges wet, folded, and worn out, and within hours it is dry, upright, and pecking. Roughly five months later a pullet lays her first egg, small and often oddly shaped, and the sealed room is built again. What is worth sitting with is not the strangeness of any one step but the tolerance of the whole system. A few degrees too cold and nothing develops. A few too warm and the chick deforms. Too little turning and it sticks. Too little water loss and it drowns in its own air cell. The chicken hits that narrow target so routinely that the process reads as ordinary, which may be the most misleading thing about it.
